content.text:
I submitted the verdict **part-based** with confidence 0.85, using 34 of the 60 budget.

**Design:** I trained the learner on two tasks, L1-S1-M1 and L2-S2-M2, so every rule it knew had appeared in only one task. Under factor-when-justified, a rule needs at least 2 trained tasks to become a reusable part, so none could have become one. Holistic and factor-when-justified therefore both predicted that tasks equally similar to the trained ones would cost the same. Part-based predicted that tasks built from already-seen rules would be cheaper.

I then tested tasks whose input-output mappings were almost completely different from both trained tasks (same response on at most 6% of inputs). Lower is cheaper:

| Task | Rules already seen | Mean examples to criterion | Tests |
|---|---|---|---|
| L2-S1-M1 | all 3 | 13.6 | 10 |
| L2-S1-M4 | 2 of 3 | 15.4 | 5 |
| L4-S4-M4 | none | 41.8 | 8 |
| L4-S3-M4 | none | 36.9 | 7 |

Tasks made from seen rules cost about a third as much as tasks with no seen rules, even though all four were equally dissimilar to what was trained. Only part-based predicts that.

**Caveats:**
- Test results were very noisy: one task ranged from 1 to 36 across repeats. The gap still held up statistically.
- I couldn't measure each task's difficulty before training, because I tested each task only once beforehand. Using two unrelated control tasks partly makes up for this.
- The task with one new rule wasn't clearly more expensive than the task with all rules seen. Cost per new rule may not be linear, but this leaves some uncertainty.
